4700.heavy: 'heavy sequence (vCC or v̄C)' --' with the macron-v glyph dropped. In the source's own terms weight is a property of vowel+consonant sequences, not syllables: a long vowel followed by a consonant (katī́r, qōnū́n, ʔahā́li) or a short vowel followed by two consonants (mánṭaqih, xalláṣt, naʔást, i.e. a closed syllable before another consonant, or a word-final -vCC). Word-final -vC and open Cv are light: bálad ~ balád and baqárih 'contain no heavy sequence'. So CVC counts as heavy only by position (non-finally, or final superheavy CVCC); coded CVV(+CVC-by-position) rather than B's coarser CVV+CVC.
4700.dflt: CvCvC: free variation between the first and the last syllable ('one hears bálad ~ balád 'village'; wálad ~ walád 'boy'; qálam ~ qalám 'pen'; šárab ~ šaráb 'he drank''), also in n-I and I-t perfects (nkásar ~ nkasár); CvCvCv: 'stress is always on the second syllable' (baqárih 'cow', šaǧárih 'tree', waráqih 'leaf', qalámu 'his pen', ħaǧáru 'his stone'), sole recorded exception sáwaʔan 'regardless whether' with initial stress. Suffixed trisyllables resyllabify to CCvCCv(C)/CvCvCCv(C) and follow the heavy-sequence rule (rqábti 'my neck', šaǧártu 'his tree').
4700.prule: Weight-sensitive rule stated with hedges. Heavy sequence = vCC (short vowel + two consonants, i.e. a non-final closed syllable or a final -vCC) or v̄C (long vowel + consonant). A word with exactly one heavy sequence is 'usually' stressed on the vowel of that sequence (mánṭaqih 'area', yášrab 'he drinks', naʔást 'I slept', katī́r 'much', ʔahā́li 'families'); a word with more than one is 'usually' stressed on the vowel of the LAST (rightmost) heavy sequence (xalláṣt 'I finished', qaddám 'opposite', qōnū́n 'law', yizzawwaǧū́n 'they marry'), with no window limit. The author immediately states that these 'cannot be considered strict rules, since many examples were recorded that go against them', naming two tendencies, regression of stress (ysáwwun ← ysuwwū́n 'they make', kátir ← katī́r, zámon ← zamā́n) and progression to the ultima (manqár ← mánqar 'chisel', yirʔáf ← yírʔaf 'he knows'), the former 'quite widespread and persistent', possibly due to dialect contact; he nevertheless 'follows' the heavy-sequence analysis with regression/progression as deviations. Heavy vCC sequences formed by the article əl-, the verbal prefix n- or the infix -t- 'usually do not draw stress' (əlbálad ~ əlbalád, not *ə́lbalad). Words without a heavy sequence: CvCvC nouns and verbs vary between initial and final stress (bálad ~ balád 'village', wálad ~ walád 'boy', šárab ~ šaráb 'he drank'); CvCvCv words are 'always' stressed on the second syllable (baqárih 'cow', šaǧárih 'tree', qalámu 'his pen'), sole recorded exception sáwaʔan 'regardless whether'; suffixed trisyllables resyllabify and follow the heavy-sequence rule (raqabih + i → rqábti 'my neck'). Phonetic correlates (§2.4.3): higher pitch; short stressed a in open Ca and final -CaC is often lengthened (balád [bəˈlaːd]), the fact Shockley 2024 cites as 'Bernabela (2011, 66)'. Accent marks on the cited forms are reconstructed from the gap positions in, which dropped the acute-accented vowels; the quote is left verbatim with those gaps.

4701.dq: No stress is described at any level. The tonal analysis is explicitly lexeme-level: 'L’analyse montre que quatre paramètres conditionnent la réalisation des tons dans le lexème' (p.174) and tonemes are identified 'sur l’axe paradigmatique au sein du lexème' (p.145).
4701.dloc: Part 'Phonétique et phonologie', ch. 3 'Système tonal', opening, p.145 and §3.4 'Conclusion', p.174
4701.prule: Tone language, no word stress described: four tonemes (high, low, rising, falling; contour tones distinctive only on monosyllabic lexemes, elsewhere only H vs L), realised on three registers with six phonetic tone levels/contours. The thesis contains no statement, section or term on word stress or accent; the only positional asymmetry reported is tonal register (lexeme-initial syllable = raising position, lexeme-final syllable = lowering position, final H realised mid).

The single use of 'accent' in any Shiwa source is Dougère 2007: 48–49, on vowel weakening: 'Cette centralisation peut aussi se retrouver en position finale et même aller jusqu’à l’élision complète de la voyelle, quand la voyelle est dénuée d’accent et donc située d…
4701.tone: Ollomo Ella 2013 (ch.3, pp.145–174, with Praat F0 measurements) treats Shiwa purely as a tone language: 6 phonetic realisations on 3 registers; 4 tonemes H, L, rising, falling; contours only on monosyllables; mid tone = final H lowered after H/voiced consonant; downtrend/uptrend and keyshift after 3 identical tones; the syllabic nasal prefix 'porte un ton bas' (p.175). A full-text search of the thesis for accent|stress|proéminen|intensité|position forte/faible finds only non-linguistic uses (fieldwork 'déstresser l’informateur', 'mettaient un accent particulier') and a bibliography title (Jouannet 1989 on Comorian). Dougère 2007 §5 'Tons' (pp.79–85) is likewise tone-only (H, B, contextual M and extra-low B+, two contours on monosyllables; analysis 'exclusivement sur les items lexicaux'); her passing remark that non-initial stem vowels are 'dénuée d’accent … position faible' implies stem-initial strength but states no accent placement. Puech 1989 (Pholia 4) has nothing on accent. Puech 1990 'Upstep in a Bantu tone language' (Pholia 5) is about li-Duma/li-Wanji (B50), not Shiwa; its p.180 West-Bantu generalisation that the radical vowel is stressed is not a Shiwa statement and is not used.

tn.quote: Le shiwa est une langue à tons. Il utilise donc les variations de la hauteur de la voix pour distinguer les ‘’mots’’. ... En shiwa, quatre tons ont une valeur distinctive: le ton haut, le ton bas, le ton montant et le ton descendant. Les tons modulés ne sont pertinents que sur les lexèmes monosyllabiques. Dans les autres cas, seuls les tons hauts et bas sont pertinents. Le ton moyen est une réalisation du ton haut en position finale si le ton précédent est haut et la consonne précédente sonore.
tn.translation: Shiwa is a tone language. It therefore uses variations in voice pitch to distinguish 'words'. ... In Shiwa, four tones have distinctive value: the high tone, the low tone, the rising tone and the falling tone. The contour (modulated) tones are relevant only on monosyllabic lexemes. In other cases only high and low tones are relevant. The mid tone is a realisation of the high tone in final position if the preceding tone is high and the preceding consonant voiced.

4703.tone: The source describes a lexical tone system only: H/M/L, six melodies (HH, MM, MH, HM, ML, HL), mora as TBU, roots bimoraic; it flags the tone analysis as preliminary ('has not been systematically studied'). Reflexes of proto-Khoe *HH/*HL/*LH/*LL are conditioned by onset type (voiced, aspirated, nasal, glottalized, ejective) and by 'narrowed' roots (Table 6, p. viii). A full-text search of the entire 46-page document for stress|accent|prominen|emphas returns nothing, so the source neither asserts nor denies word stress. Family-level context (Google Books of Vossen 1997, Die Khoe-Sprachen): 'Ebenfalls noch weitgehend ungeklärt ist die Frage, ob Druckakzent distinktive Funktion in den Khoe-Sprachen zukommt' (whether stress has distinctive function in Khoe languages is still largely unresolved); Vossen's concrete stress remarks (stress on the root vowel in finite verb forms of tone classes 2, 3, 5; tone classes 1 and 4 pass stress to the juncture; primary + secondary stress in >2-syllable verbs) sit in the ǁAni (§4.3.1.2.2, p. 179) and ǂHaba (before §3.5, p. 113) sections, not in the Shua sections. Vossen 2013 (Khoesan Languages, p. 103, excerpt): 'Very little is known about tone systems in Shua languages. In Cara, surface analysis has established H(igh) and L(ow) as essential level tones combining to H-H, L-L, H-L, and L-H as tonal sequences on CVCV, CVV and CVN'.

4705.prule: No word-stress rule is stated by any reachable source. Siamou is described as a tone language: Toews 2015 (§1.2, §2.2) has three level tones H, M, L plus downstepped !H and contour melodies (HL, H!H, M!HL), tone being lexically and grammatically contrastive; Prost 1964 (§§9-11) has two extreme tones (high, low) plus two intermediate levels (four basic levels, 'il n'y a pas un ton moyen'), a fifth level used only for the plural of tone-4 words, and falling contours. Stress appears only indirectly: Toews, after Traoré 1984 and Nicolson 2010, says the reduced vowel [ə] occurs only in unstressed syllables, and Traoré's four disyllabic examples carry a stress mark before the second (final) syllable while the unstressed first syllable still bears tone; Prost mentions an 'accent d'intensité' once, as one of two possible triggers of a rare glottal after a/ã, with no placement.

4705.tone: Toews 2015 §1.2 (p. 8): 'Tones are usually marked with an accent on the vowel of the syllable in which they occur. High tone (H) is marked e.g. á, low tone (L) e.g. à. mid tones (M, M(L), M(!H)) are unmarked. A high-low contour tone (HL) is marked e.g. â. A high-downstepped-high contour tone (H!H) is marked áa, and a rising-falling contour (M!HL) by a sequence of two vowels'; §2.2 (pp. 23-36) gives H/M/L plus !H and eight tone melodies; aspectual suffixes fall into L, M and HL tonal classes. Prost 1964 §§9-11: two extreme tones plus two intermediate tones (numbered 1-4 from the bottom), a fifth non-modulated tone for the plural of tone 4, and falling contours whose mechanics were not determined. On stress/accent: Toews (reporting Traoré 1984:80 and Nicolson 2010) says [ə] occurs only in unstressed syllables and Traoré's four disyllables are marked with stress on the second syllable (/mə́'kâl/, /kə̀'jɛ̃ᵑ/, /gbə'kɛl/, /tə'kpâr/), the unstressed syllable still carrying H or L tone; no placement rule is stated and Toews does not discuss stress elsewhere in 410 pp. (full-text search for stress/accent/prominence). Prost mentions only an 'accent d'intensité' as a possible trigger of a rare glottal after a/ã. Vogler 2015 (p. 2) calls Sèmè a 'système tonal à quatre registres'; Toews 2010 fn. 3 gives the tone orthography only.

4708.prule: No word-level stress: all syllables of a simple or compound word are evenly stressed, affixes and stems alike; stress is never distinctive ('not used to differentiate the meaning of disyllabic words'). Lexical pitch is carried by three tones (high-level, mid-level, low-falling).
4708.srule: Not mentioned in Fu 1997 [1950], II.(4) Stress §71, pp. 63-64: all syllables of simple and compound words are evenly stressed, so there is no within-word stress gradation (primary or secondary) to place.
4708.quote: 71. Syllables of a simple or compound word are evenly stressed no matter whether they are affixes or stem words. Thus, in ²a ²ʂo 'long', the prefix ²a has the same stress as the stem word ²ʂo; in the compound ²ia ²ka ¹pi ²du 'pipe-cleaner', the constituent words ²ia ²ka and ¹pi have the same stress as the particle ²du. 4708.tone: Three tones in the Pei-shan dialect used 'as primary phonemes' (§68: 1 high-level ¹he 'to stand', 2 mid-level ²he 'arrow', 3 low-falling ³he 'to speak'); tone values unchanged in sentences except third -> second tone on the reduplicated syllable of interrogatives (§69); no rule relates tones to initials or prefixes (§70). Stress, unlike tone, never distinguishes meaning; emphatic stress raises pitch and unstressed lowers it (§71).

tn.quote: Sidaama is a pitch-accent language, which indicates prominence with high pitch. ... First, Sidaama is actually a pitch-accent language, where prominence is indicated by high pitch, rather than stress. The location of high pitch in a word is predictable, and high pitch is not associated with the duration of a vowel. Second, the pitch-accent patterns in Sidaama cannot be described by syllables as easily as by segments (or moras; see section 2.3.1). In Sidaama, high pitch is normally assigned to the second to the last vowel segment of the citation form of an open-class word.
tn.cite: Kawachi 2013, Mermaid constructions in Sidaama (NINJAL), sec. 3 p. 573 [primary citation]; with Kawachi 2007, A grammar of Sidaama (Sidamo), PhD diss. Univ. at Buffalo, ch. 2 sec. 2.3.2 'Pitch Accent' pp. 63-71 (same author's reference grammar, cited on p. 573)

4713.prule: Two-register (high vs low) tone language; register is largely predictable from the word-initial consonant, pitch is the decisive cue where it is not. Heavy = long vowel or coda consonant per Van der Mark 2002:181 summarising Kaneko 1999 ('heavy syllables are those with a long vowel or a consonant in the coda'); Van Der Mark 2003:12 adds that a word-final consonant is not moraic.
4714.dflt: Lexically specified: 'If there is no heavy syllable, prominence is lexically specified... There do not appear to be any phonological rules to predict where the prominence will fall in words with only light syllables' (Van der Mark 2002:181, reporting Kaneko 1999; second-hand for Kaneko).
4714.prule: Lexical pitch accent, no positional stress rule: each word typically carries one lexically specified high-pitch accent (acute in Frantz's orthography), on a long or short vowel, at no position computable from syllable count or word edge; no word is accentless; a few polymorphemic words (compounds, verb complexes) carry more than one accent. Weight is a tendency only: accent 'tends to fall on heavy syllables' (Kaneko 1999) with 'numerous exceptions'.
4714.srule: None described: 'Blackfoot words typically contain one pitch accent... multiple PAs uncommon, occurring in a few types of poly-morphemic words such as compounds or verb complexes'; as a pitch-accent language, no 'secondary word-level prominence' and no alternating rhythm (Van Der Mark 2003:11, 20). No placement is given for the extra accents. Later Siksika data show multi-accent (and accentless) words more widely (Stacy 2004:69-70, 75-76) and Weber 2020:177 leaves possible secondary stresses in longer phonological phrases unanalysed; no source states a secondary-stress rule.

4714.tone: Van Der Mark 2003 classifies Blackfoot as a pitch-accent language, not a stress language: §3.4 'Definitions' p. 21 defines PA languages as those 'that modulate only pitch in marking a phonologically prominent syllable', and the conclusion (p. 103) speaks of 'a pitch accent language such as Blackfoot or Japanese'; instrumentally F0 is the main correlate, intensity and duration are also raised, and Glottal Skew (vocal-fold tension, the stress correlate) 'is not correlated with Blackfoot PA'. Accent placement is lexical ('primarily lexical'); Elfner 2006:14: 'Blackfoot is a pitch accent language... Unlike stress, accent placement in Blackfoot is virtually unpredictable, although some generalisations exist'. Dissent: Stacy 2004 (abstract p. iii, pp. 1-2) argues Blackfoot 'lacks significant metrical features' and is a tonal system, citing 'severe breaches of culminativity, with cases of up to four accents per word'. Either way no source states a word-stress rule.

4721.tone: Naorem 2009: 'Being a Tibeto-Burman language, Simte also has the tonal system. There are two tones in Simte, viz. (a) falling tone /ˋ/ and (b) level tone /ˉ/. Falling tone is marked and level tone is not marked.'; 'In this language, tones are limited although some words do have.' Minimal pairs, level vs falling, read from (p. 49): ɟu 'rat'/ɟù 'wine', ni 'aunt'/nǐ 'day', si 'die'/sǐ 'blood', ŋa 'five'/ŋà 'fish', ləy 'tongue'/lə̀y 'bridge', si-al 'fox'/sǐal 'mithun', la 'take'/là 'song', ha 'month'/hà 'teeth'; (p. 50): məy 'fire'/mə̀y 'tail', sun 'mid-day'/sùn 'mourn', thəw 'fat'/thə̀w 'rise', peh 'kick'/pèh 'broad', kəy 'I'/kə̀y 'bite', lam 'dance'/làm 'wealth', bel 'pot'/bèl 'help', gəmla 'flower'/gəmlà 'distance'. (The p. 50 glosses kəy 'I'/kə̀y 'bite' and lam 'dance'/làm 'wealth' are as printed; A's 'kay dance/bite' and 'lam -/wealth' were an scan column shift. The initial of the first pair is the voiced palatal plosive /ɟ/ of Table 3, p. 17, not /j/; A and B both wrote ju.) The words stress, accent, prominence, intonation and pitch do not occur in the chapter except in the Clark & Yallop tone definition quoted on p. 49 (nor in the Ch. I or bibliography scan). Kapginlian 2025 (Morpho Syntax of Simte, NEHU PhD, ch. 2 pp. 116-118), citing Ching 2022, instead reports 'four tones as contrast to Singh (2009) findings' -- 'Register tones: mid [ˉ] and low tone [ˋ], and two Contour tones: falling rising [ˇ] and rising falling [ˆ] (Ching, 2022, p.76)'…

4723.dq: ' shows where the accent falls: in the absence of any mark the accent falls on the penultimate syllable. [A key to wordlist citation forms; 'word' is never named and no Singa phrase-level or word-level description exists.]
4723.dloc: Johnston 1904 vol. 2, p. 901; Lusinga column pp. 993-1000; locale line p. 993. Johnston 1919 vol. 1 p. 41.
4723.prule: No Singa-specific statement exists. The only stress-related text is Johnston's volume-wide transcription key (p. 901), applying to all fifty vocabularies (Nilotic, Masai, Somali and Bantu alike): an acute marks the accented syllable, and an unmarked word is accented on the penultimate syllable. Under that convention the ~70 unmarked Lusinga items (Johnston reprints about half of Hobley's 142 filled entries) are implicitly penult-accented and one item, Mwanámtu 'child' (compound mwana + mtu), is marked antepenult. But the Lusinga list is Hobley's 1902 list reprinted (Hobley's printing has no accent marks and no pronunciation key), so the macrons and the single acute are Johnston's editorial additions to data he did not collect; the convention is not an observation about Singa.
4723.srule: Not mentioned in Johnston 1904 vol. 2 (orthography key p. 901; Lusinga vocabulary pp. 993-1000): the key supplies one accent mark per word and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress; Hobley 1902 pp. 92-95 and Johnston 1919 vol. 1 p. 41 are likewise silent.

4725.dq: Sipakapense has adopted this process of dropping vowels before stress (which generally falls on the last syllable of a word).
4725.heavy: Not applicable: Barrett 2002 calls the system 'quantity-insensitive'; a long vowel in a non-final syllable is unstressed (iiʃáq, kiib'ék: long first syllable, stress on the short final) and the final syllable is stressed whether its vowel is long (iʃiím) or short (atʃí, b'án, kiib'ék).
4725.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive: Barrett 1996 'generally falls on the last syllable of a word'; Barrett 2002 'quantity-insensitive R → L iambs' with final acute in every example (atʃí, iiʃáq, kiib'ék, ʃkàtktsulíχ, ʃkatìntsulíχ, kuwìts'ulíχ, kùχuwìts'ulíχ).
4725.srule: Barrett 2002: 7 characterises the system as 'quantity-insensitive R → L iambs', and ex. (14) marks secondary stress (grave accent; notation defined p. 1: 'primary stress marked = ó, secondary stress = ò') on every second syllable leftward of the final primary, including the initial syllable of odd-parity words: ʃkàtktsulíχ (3 syllables, 101), kuwìts'ulíχ and ʃkatìntsulíχ (4, 0101), kùχuwìts'ulíχ (5, 10101); the disyllables atʃí, iiʃáq, kiib'ék carry no grave (01). The alternation is strictly syllabic in every printed form. Barrett 1996 marks no secondary stress.
